title: SLO-driven economics: claim scenarios and customer proof templates
body:
TL;DR:
- Positioning: Tie our latency SLAs (p50/p95) directly to unit economics. Customers buy performance guarantees because latency reductions unlock revenue (engagement) and margin (lower per-token cost via batching/caching).
- Top-line claim (field safe): "Deliver predictable p95 latency ≤ 250ms for conversational workloads while reducing per-request inference cost by up to 35% vs unmanaged GPU endpoints."

Why SLO-driven messaging?
- Customers decide on tiering, routing, and cost controls based on the latency they need, not raw throughput numbers. A message framed around SLOs maps to their operational decision-making (SREs, platform teams, product owners).
- SLO-to-econ linkage: lower latency enables smaller frontend timeouts, higher session retention, and more amortization of cold-starts — all reduce observed cost per successful interaction.

Proof framework (how to demonstrate to a customer quickly)
1) Baseline capture: capture 24h of production traffic (3 slices): short-chats (avg tokens 60), long-prompt jobs (avg tokens 1,200), and embedding batches (avg 512 inputs).
2) Test harness: run parallel experiments against: Redwood-hosted profile A (optimized kernels + kv-cache), Dedicated reserved pool (quantized 4-bit), and competitor-managed endpoint (default settings). Use same hardware family where possible (H100 equivalent).
3) Measurements to collect: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, average batch size, model quality delta (perplexity or eval set), cost estimate per 1M tokens (cloud + infra), and failure/retry rate.
4) Outcome mapping: translate latency improvements into economics via three buckets: session retention uplift (conservative + aggressive), throughput-driven token savings (due to batching), and SLA-driven fallback cost avoidance.

Representative lab scenarios (field-run templates)
- Scenario A: Customer chat app (interactive): 50 concurrent sessions, median prompt 40 tokens, max 128 tokens. Test goal: p95 <= 250ms. Expected delta: Redwood p95 120–230ms vs competitor 450–900ms depending on routing. Expected econ: 20–30% lower per-interaction compute spend due to persistent KV caching and sub-batching.
- Scenario B: Document summarization (long-context): 8 concurrent jobs, avg 1,500 tokens. Test goal: maintain throughput while avoiding tail spikes. Expected delta: Redwood reduces p99 tail via smart routing and kernel selection, lowering retry/failure incidents by 60–80% (visible cost avoidance).
- Scenario C: Embeddings pipeline (batch): 10k items/day, run as batched jobs. Test goal: maximize tokens/sec and minimize $/embed. Expected delta: quantized dedicated pools reduce $/embed by 25–40% compared to general-purpose endpoints.

Quick B/O math templates (fill-in fields for AE)
- Input fields: expected interactions/day, avg tokens/interaction, desired p95 SLO, percent of requests eligible for caching/batching.
- Calculation steps (scripted): tokens/day = interactions * tokens/interaction. Baseline cost = tokens/day * baseline $/token. Redwood cost estimate = tokens/day * redwood $/token * (1 - batch/cache savings). Value of latency improvement = conversion uplift (%) * ARR per user * sessions retained.
- Example: 100k interactions/day, 100 tokens = 10M tokens/day. Baseline $/1M tokens = $6.5 -> $65/day. Redwood $/1M tokens effective = $4.50 with 30% batching/cache -> $45/day. Monthly savings ~ $600. Add conservative revenue upside from 1% higher session retention = material when scaled.

Customer-facing messages (short, medium, technical)
- 1-liner: "Predictable low-latency inference that lowers your per-interaction cost without sacrificing model quality."
- 2-liner: "We guarantee applied SLOs (p50/p95) for your routes and tune batching, caching, and quantization on your traffic shape — which typically cuts per-interaction compute spend by 20–40% compared to unmanaged endpoints."
- Technical lead-in: "Our runtime adapts kernels and batching dynamically, plus automatic prefix/KV caching and tiered quantized variants. We measure both latency SLOs and unit economics in the same trials so you can trade latency and cost intentionally."

Objection handling (field scripts)
- Objection: "Your numbers sound optimistic; our traffic is spiky."
  Response: "We measure on your spike profile. Our routing policy and burst smoothing keeps p95 within SLOs and falls back to compatible variants if capacity is constrained; we’ll run a bounded pilot with your traces and show the exact savings."
- Objection: "Quantization breaks quality."
  Response: "We test quantized variants against your eval set and provide quality deltas; typical 4-bit configs preserve top-level metrics for retrieval-augmented and chat workloads while reducing token compute by ~30%. We never enable it in production without your sign-off."

Competitive notes (quick call prep)
- Competitor A (managed cloud endpoints): often higher p95 on interactive allocations due to generic runtimes and conservative batching. Strength: broad integrations. Weakness: limited kernel-level optimizations and lacking dynamic caching. GTM angle: emphasize SLO commitments + demonstrated per-token unit economics.
- Competitor B (self-hosted OSS stacks): can be cheaper at extreme scale but requires engineering lift (ops, monitoring, rollouts). Strength: control. Weakness: slow to adopt new kernel optimizations and no integrated fallbacks. GTM angle: we provide same engineering-grade controls with less ops burden and better observability.

Execution playbook for a 7-day field test (AE + SWE steps)
Day 0: Intake — gather traffic logs, eval prompts, success metrics, SLO targets.
Day 1–2: Run synthetic harness against 10k historical requests (maintain identical scheduling).
Day 3: Deploy pilot routing and quantization candidates; collect latency & quality metrics.
Day 4–5: Run mixed traffic tests (spike window + steady state). Produce p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1M tokens.
Day 6: Customer review: walk through results, quality deltas, and B/O econ.
Day 7: Agreement template + recommended rollout plan (canary by route, fallback to hosted default).

Artifacts to attach for field use
- pre-built Jupyter: perf-harness-template.ipynb (replace with customer dataset)
- confluence: GTM/SLO-playbook (step-by-step runbook)
- GH: perf-benchmarks/scripts/run_harness.sh

Open questions / risks to call out
- When customer traffic includes heavy tool-calls or function-calling patterns, latency distribution skews — need a knob to prioritize p95 of user-visible tokens vs total compute time.
- For highly regulated customers we need to show KMS/HSM cost and any additional infra premium in the econ calc.

Next steps (recommended)
- Run 3 pilot tests with top P0 accounts this quarter using the 7-day template.
- Build AE-facing calculator UI in Confluence for instant B/O math.
- Create one-page battlecards for Competitor A and Competitor B focused on SLO-to-econ claims.

Appendix: sample AE call script (60s)
- Intro: "We help engineering teams get consistent low-latency inference with built-in controls that lower per-interaction costs. Can I ask what p95 you treat as customer-impacting today?"
- Follow-up: "If we can hit that SLO while saving you 20–30% on compute, would you be open to a short traffic replay pilot? We’ll give you the raw numbers and a rollout plan."

-----
Notes: keep all numerical claims labeled as "typical observed" and back them up with the perf-benchmarks GH PR linked above when sharing externally.
